title: The Ten Commandments (CCC 2052–2074)
hook: two tablets: love of God, love of neighbor; Catholics number them as Augustine did

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. Your line was the hinges. Which one did you use? Today, the oldest moral list in the Bible, and a question of counting. Day three hundred fifteen.

Ask a room full of people to list the Ten Commandments and something funny happens. Everyone gets thou shalt not kill and thou shalt not steal. Then it gets vague. Someone says be nice to your parents. Someone says no idols, and someone else says that's not one of them, and a friendly argument starts about what number seven is. Both sides might be right. Christians and Jews have counted the same verses in different ways for a very long time. Before the counting, though, there's a mountain, a people just freed from slavery, and a voice.
screen: `EVERYONE GETS KILL AND STEAL.` → `WHAT NUMBER IS SEVEN?` → `A MOUNTAIN, AND A VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, how it begins. Not with a rule. With a rescue. In the Douay-Rheims, God says: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." The commandments are given to people who've just been set free, as the way to stay free. Second, the word. Decalogue is Greek for ten words. The Bible itself calls them the ten words, in Hebrew aseret ha-devarim. Third, the two tablets. Moses comes down with two tablets of stone. The Church, following Augustine, puts three commandments on the first, about loving God: no other gods, honoring God's name, keeping the Lord's day holy. And seven on the second, about loving neighbor: honor your parents, don't kill, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't covet your neighbor's wife, don't covet your neighbor's goods. Jesus sums up both tablets when he's asked for the greatest commandment: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart," and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two tablets, one love. Fourth, the counting. Catholics and Lutherans follow Augustine: no other gods and no images as one commandment, and coveting split into two. Orthodox and many other Protestant churches count the images as a separate second commandment, and coveting as one. Jewish tradition counts I am the Lord thy God as the first word. The verses are the same. Each tradition counts them its own way, and none of them leaves anything out. This week walked from freedom and conscience, through sin, the Beatitudes and the virtues, to the ten words.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH A RESCUE.` · `DECALOGUE: TEN WORDS.` · `THREE FOR GOD, SEVEN FOR NEIGHBOR.` · `SAME VERSES, COUNTED DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TWO TABLETS, ONE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Exodus 20, verses 1 to 17. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, open it and read slowly, all seventeen verses. It takes about two minutes. If you can't, simply walk through the ten in your head, three for God, seven for neighbor, and stop at the one that catches. Don't grade yourself. Just notice which word speaks to your week. If you pray, you can bring that one to God. The bell holds the time.
Decalogue. Greek for ten words: the Ten Commandments given at Sinai, which Jesus summed up as love of God and love of neighbor. Today's word.
Your line: two tablets, one love. Today, pick the commandment that caught you, and keep it in one small, concrete way. Day three hundred fifteen.
